independence_scope: intra-mesh Anthropic-family; agreement is corroboration, never cross-provider evidence

reviews.reasoning: Span re-derived independently. Numbering: Ps 110 is an identity psalm (web_mt_offset_map; the superscription inventory records mt_title_verses 'prefix_of_v1', labels mizmor + le_david), so web:Ps.110.0 = oshb:Ps.110.1 and web:Ps.110.1 = oshb:Ps.110.1 both resolve to MT 110:1; citation_sweep.py returns GREEN on the row's refs and check_tiling.py tiles Ps.110.1-Ps.114.8 at 44/44 verses with no gap or overlap. All 4 Hebrew runs in this row collate at BYTE tier (collate.py: 4/4 byte, 0 below byte). The opening warrant is sound and I do not contest the span: a skeleton sweep of the oracle formula returns 1 verse book-wide (oshb:Ps.110.1) and of the oath formula 2 verses (oshb:Ps.110.4, oshb:Ps.132.11), so the 110:3|110:4 seam rests on a genuinely distinctive tier-1 speech frame rather than on taste. pmarks_Ps.json records no selah, no K/Q and no puncta anywhere in Ps 110-114, so no disclosure obligation is outstanding; the one paseq at MT 110:1 is seg-layer and the row makes no claim about it. Two defects remain in the row's own evidence, both byte-checkable: the discourse-person characterisation of vv2-3 is wrong in both witnesses, and the 110:1 gloss covers less than the Hebrew span it is attached to. Confidence 'high' is otherwise defensible for this seam.

challenges.claim: The row calls Ps 110:2-3 'third-person description' in both the rationale and observed_substrate_signals, but both verses are second-person address to the same addressee, with 6 second-masculine-singular forms and an imperative across the two verses.
challenges.evidence: Byte splices from verse_map_oshb.json, each glossed over the same span from the WEB: עֻזְּךָ֗ (oshb:Ps.110.2, web:Ps.110.2 “the rod of your strength”) and רְ֝דֵ֗ה בְּקֶ֣רֶב אֹיְבֶֽיךָ (oshb:Ps.110.2, web:Ps.110.2 “Rule among your enemies”); עַמְּךָ֣ (oshb:Ps.110.3, web:Ps.110.3 “Your people offer themselves willingly”), חֵ֫ילֶ֥ךָ (oshb:Ps.110.3, web:Ps.110.3 “in the day of your power”) and לְ֝ךָ֗ טַ֣ל יַלְדֻתֶֽיךָ (oshb:Ps.110.3, web:Ps.110.3 “you have the dew of your youth”). That is 2 second-person forms in MT 110:2 plus a second-person imperative, and 4 in MT 110:3 — 6 second-person-suffixed forms across the 2 verses, 0 third-person references to the addressee. Both witnesses agree; the WEB renders every one of them as 'your'/'you'. The staged extract carries no morphology layer, so the imperative reading of the third slice is argued from the pointed bytes plus both renderings, but the suffixed forms are orthographic and need no morphology. The row's warrant that the unit is held together by continuity of register therefore rests on a mis-stated register: vv1-3 are one stretch of second-person address opened by the oracle, not an oracle followed by third-person description. observed_substrate_signals is a dependent field of that characterisation and carries the same error.

challenges.claim: The 110:1 Hebrew quote and its gloss do not cover the same span: the quoted Hebrew runs through the two-word direct command, while the gloss stops at the speech-introduction.
challenges.evidence: The row quotes MT 110:1 from the oracle formula through שֵׁ֥ב לִֽימִינִ֑י (oshb:Ps.110.1) but glosses the whole run as web:Ps.110.1 “Yahweh says to my Lord”, which renders only the first three words. The WEB for the trailing 2 words of the quoted span is web:Ps.110.1 “Sit at my right hand”. Quote/gloss parity is a campaign rule in both directions — the repair re-cuts the gloss (or the quote), and the row's own second unit does it correctly, glossing its full Hebrew run with two WEB segments.

reviews.reasoning: Span and seam re-derived. The oath frame at MT 110:4 is a real tier-1 opener: a skeleton sweep of the two-word oath formula returns 2 verses book-wide (oshb:Ps.110.4, oshb:Ps.132.11) against 1 verse for the oracle formula at oshb:Ps.110.1, so the 110:3|110:4 cut is well warranted and I do not contest the span or the rejected_alternative. All 4 Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier. The row's central original-language 'finding', however, is an artifact claim: it reads the absence of maqaf in the staged bytes as a fact about the text, at exactly the verse the byte-verified source-view erratum names as the example of what may NOT be claimed. A second signal mis-states the discourse person of the span's first verse, and the device_notes name a campaign authoring artifact in row prose. check_marks.py and citation_sweep.py are GREEN on this row; pmarks_Ps.json shows 1 paseq at MT 110:4 (seg layer, uncited and unclaimed here, correctly).

challenges.claim: The row converts a known extraction artifact into a textual claim, asserting that the source bytes carry no maqaf in the Melchizedek phrase 'contrary to a hyphenated rendering' and that this is 'verified across all 4 tiers'.
challenges.evidence: The staged OSHB extract serializes maqaf as a SPACE — 0 maqaf codepoints across all 2527 MT verses — while the OSHB XML carries 2404 x-maqqef segs; the byte-verified source-view erratum names this exact verse ('Melchizedek at MT 110:4') as a WLC print-tradition claim that is NOT a claim about the quotable bytes, and rules that maqaf must never be asserted in quoted spans. The four tiers are not independent here: byte, nfd, accent_stripped and skeleton all derive from the same maqaf-free serialization, so 'verified across all 4 tiers' adds no evidence. The row's own space is indistinguishable from every other space in the verse: עַל דִּ֝בְרָתִ֗י and מַלְכִּי צֶֽדֶק (oshb:Ps.110.4) are separated by the same U+0020 as the two words inside each pair, and the whole run is glossed web:Ps.110.4 “in the order of Melchizedek”. The correct handling is to make no maqaf claim in either direction, or to cite the XML seg layer; as written the row states a positive textual fact the staged source cannot support, and it occupies an observed_substrate_signals slot and the device_notes with it.

challenges.claim: The signal 'third-person royal-warfare description runs oshb:Ps.110.5-Ps.110.7' is false at the first verse of the range, which is second-person address.
challenges.evidence: אֲדֹנָ֥י עַל יְמִֽינְךָ֑ (oshb:Ps.110.5) carries the second-masculine-singular suffix on the last word and is rendered web:Ps.110.5 “The Lord is at your right hand”. MT 110:6 and 110:7 are indeed third-person, so the accurate scope of the signal is 2 of the 3 verses named, not 3. This matters because the row's stated warrant for holding vv4-7 together is uninterrupted third-person continuation after the oath; the actual continuity is that the second-person addressee of the oath is still being addressed in v5 before the description turns.

challenges.claim: device_notes names a campaign authoring artifact in row prose ('the seam the part brief flags for byte-settlement before any ordinal claim'), which the register rule bans from row prose.
challenges.evidence: The register rule admits no decision-ids, strategy-section citations, erratum narration, positional row references, file-order talk or review-actor names in row prose EVER; a reference to 'the part brief' is the same class of pipeline artifact and is not a statement about the text. ngram7.py confirms the phrasing is not isolated — the 7-gram 'web ps is the seam the part' recurs across 2 rows of this cluster. The cure is one edit per row: state the textual fact (the oath frame at MT 110:4) without naming the instrument that asked for it.

reviews.reasoning: The whole_psalm verdict for Ps 111 is right and I support the span: the acrostic is colon-level (22 cola over 10 verses per the device inventory scheme_note), verse-initial hallelu-Yah is recorded for oshb:Ps.111.1 in the inventory's 11-member verse-initial list with no verse-final member for this psalm (the 13-member verse-final list contains oshb:Ps.113.9 but nothing in Ps 111), and there is no addressee or refrain shift inside the psalm. All 4 Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier. But the row's two supporting evidence blocks are both wrong at the byte/arithmetic level, and the sentence carrying the warrant is the inverse of what the letters do. I re-derived the letter table from consonantal_index.json skeletons and from the inventory's acrostics entry rather than from the row.

challenges.claim: The row states that the clause it quotes from MT 111:3 recurs at oshb:Ps.112.9 and attaches 'sweep: 3 of 3 skeleton hits book-wide' to it, but the quoted clause does not occur at MT 112:9 at any tier, and the 3-verse count belongs to a different swept object.
challenges.evidence: collate.py on the row's own quoted string against oshb:Ps.112.9 returns tier 'none' (not byte, not nfd, not accent_stripped, not skeleton). The reason is orthographic and visible in the bytes: וְ֝צִדְקָת֗וֹ עֹמֶ֥דֶת לָעַֽד (oshb:Ps.111.3, web:Ps.111.3 “His righteousness endures forever”) and וְ֝צִדְקָת֗וֹ עֹמֶ֥דֶת לָעַֽד (oshb:Ps.112.3, web:Ps.112.3 “His righteousness endures forever”) open with the conjunction, while צִ֭דְקָתוֹ עֹמֶ֣דֶת לָעַ֑ד (oshb:Ps.112.9, web:Ps.112.9 “His righteousness endures forever”) does not. Named-object sweeps with sweep.py (count_unit = verses): the conjunction-initial spelling returns 2 verses (Ps.111.3, Ps.112.3); the conjunction-less spelling returns 3 verses (Ps.111.3, Ps.112.3, Ps.112.9); the bare predicate alone returns 4 verses (Ps.111.3, Ps.111.10, Ps.112.3, Ps.112.9). The row names the 2-verse object and reports the 3-verse figure. The 4-verse figure also matters to the argument the row is making: the same predicate closes this psalm at תְּ֝הִלָּת֗וֹ עֹמֶ֥דֶת לָעַֽד (oshb:Ps.111.10, web:Ps.111.10 “His praise endures forever!”), so the clause is not exclusive to the 111/112 pairing.

challenges.claim: The row's description of the acrostic series is wrong at three checkable points: it calls the series 'the verse-opening letters' when the first member is not verse-initial, it places resh at alphabet position 19, and it describes the non-verse-initial residue as 'the missing even-position letters plus the closing tav'.
challenges.evidence: (1) MT 111:1 opens הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ (oshb:Ps.111.1, web:Ps.111.1 “Praise Yah!”) — the raw verse-initial letter is he, and the acrostic's aleph is the third word, אוֹדֶ֣ה יְ֭הוָה בְּכָל לֵבָ֑ב (oshb:Ps.111.1, web:Ps.111.1 “I will give thanks to Yahweh with my whole heart”). The inventory's first_letters_mt string is explicitly V1_STRIP-normalized for 111/112 (its own derivation note says the title prefix is stripped at v1 for 25/37/111/112/145 and instructs citers to say which layer they mean); the row cites the normalized layer under a raw-layer description. (2) Alphabet positions of the series aleph, gimel, he, zayin, tet, kaf, mem, samekh, pe, resh are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 20 — resh is the 20th letter, qof is the 19th. So the series is not 'the odd-position letters' either: 9 of its 10 members are odd-position, the 10th is even. (3) The inventory's letters_missing for Ps 111 is bet, dalet, waw, het, yod, lamed, nun, ayin, tsade, qof, shin, tav = positions 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 19, 21, 22; qof (19) and shin (21) are odd and missing, and tav is itself position 22, i.e. even — so 'the missing even-position letters plus the closing tav' misdescribes the set in two directions. (4) The same sentence says the interlocking second colon 'sits mid-verse', but MT 111:9 and 111:10 each carry TWO mid-verse letters, not one: פְּד֤וּת שָׁ֘לַ֤ח לְעַמּ֗וֹ / צִוָּֽה לְעוֹלָ֥ם בְּרִית֑וֹ / קָד֖וֹשׁ וְנוֹרָ֣א שְׁמֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.111.9, web:Ps.111.9 “He has sent redemption to his people”, “He has ordained his covenant forever”, “His name is holy and awesome!”) and רֵ֘אשִׁ֤ית חָכְמָ֨ה יִרְאַ֬ת יְהוָ֗ה / שֵׂ֣כֶל ט֭וֹב לְכָל עֹשֵׂיהֶ֑ם / תְּ֝הִלָּת֗וֹ עֹמֶ֥דֶת לָעַֽד (oshb:Ps.111.10, web:Ps.111.10 “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom”, “All those who do his work have a good understanding”, “His praise endures forever!”) — 3 cola each, which is exactly how 10 verses carry 22 cola.

challenges.claim: The sentence carrying the whole_psalm warrant asserts the inverse of the byte data: it says no verse boundary inside the psalm corresponds to a letter-boundary, whereas each of the 9 internal verse boundaries opens a new acrostic letter.
challenges.evidence: Verse-initial letters re-derived from consonantal_index.json skeletons, one per verse: he (v1, the strip-normalized aleph at word 3), gimel (v2, גְּ֭דֹלִים מַעֲשֵׂ֣י יְהוָ֑ה oshb:Ps.111.2, web:Ps.111.2 “Yahweh’s works are great”), he (v3), zayin (v4), tet (v5), kaf (v6), mem (v7), samekh (v8), pe (v9, פְּד֤וּת שָׁ֘לַ֤ח לְעַמּ֗וֹ oshb:Ps.111.9, web:Ps.111.9 “He has sent redemption to his people”), resh (v10, רֵ֘אשִׁ֤ית חָכְמָ֨ה יִרְאַ֬ת יְהוָ֗ה oshb:Ps.111.10, web:Ps.111.10 “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom”). All 9 internal boundaries (v1|v2 through v9|v10) coincide with a new acrostic letter; 0 of them fall inside a letter. The defensible form of the warrant is the opposite observation — because each of the 10 verses takes a letter and no letter GROUP is set off, the letter series privileges no internal seam over any other, which is why the psalm is not cuttable on acrostic evidence. As written, a reviewer who checks the bytes finds the stated reason false while the conclusion happens to survive; the replacement warrant has to pass the test that killed this one.

reviews.reasoning: I support the whole_psalm span and the typed-relation handling of the 111/112 pairing: both psalms carry their own 22-cola scheme (device inventory scheme_note for 111 and 112, identical first_letters_mt strings), oshb:Ps.112.1 is in the inventory's 11-member verse-initial hallelu-Yah list, and merging the two would cross a psalm boundary, which row policy forbids. All 5 Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier (collate.py: 5 of 5 byte) and citation_sweep.py is GREEN, including the web:Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10 range ref. Two defects: the row asserts byte-identity across three sites where collate.py gives two different answers, and it repeats the letter-boundary warrant whose byte basis is the inverse of the claim. Confidence 'high' is over-set for a row whose stated byte evidence does not collate as stated.

challenges.claim: The row prints the MT 112:9 form and the MT 112:3 form and then says all 3 sites 'share the same clause, byte-identical, with oshb:Ps.111.3', but MT 112:9 matches the other two only at skeleton tier, and the accompanying 'sweep: 3 of 3 skeleton hits book-wide' is attached to a spelling that yields 2 verses.
challenges.evidence: collate.py, run on strings spliced from verse_map_oshb.json: the conjunction-initial clause וְ֝צִדְקָת֗וֹ עֹמֶ֥דֶת לָעַֽד (oshb:Ps.111.3, web:Ps.111.3 “His righteousness endures forever”) collates byte against oshb:Ps.112.3 and 'none' against oshb:Ps.112.9; the conjunction-less clause צִ֭דְקָתוֹ עֹמֶ֣דֶת לָעַ֑ד (oshb:Ps.112.9, web:Ps.112.9 “His righteousness endures forever”) collates byte against oshb:Ps.112.9 but only SKELETON against oshb:Ps.111.3 and oshb:Ps.112.3. The two sites that are byte-identical are oshb:Ps.111.3 and וְ֝צִדְקָת֗וֹ עֹמֶ֥דֶת לָעַֽד (oshb:Ps.112.3, web:Ps.112.3 “His righteousness endures forever”) — 2 sites, not 3. Named-object sweeps (sweep.py, count_unit = verses): conjunction-initial spelling 2 verses; conjunction-less spelling 3 verses; bare predicate 4 verses (the fourth is oshb:Ps.111.10). 'byte-identical' is reserved for what collate.py returns as byte, with the tier named; the correct statement is that the pairing runs across 3 verses at skeleton tier and 2 of them at byte tier.

challenges.claim: The row repeats the false letter-boundary warrant, asserting that no verse boundary inside Ps 112 aligns with a letter-boundary, when each of the 9 internal boundaries opens a new acrostic letter.
challenges.evidence: Verse-initial letters of Ps 112 re-derived from consonantal_index.json skeletons: he (v1, strip-normalized aleph at word 3 — the psalm opens הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ in the same shape as oshb:Ps.111.1, and web:Ps.112.1 reads “Praise Yah!” before “Blessed is the man who fears Yahweh”), then gimel, he, zayin, tet, kaf, mem, samekh, pe, resh at vv2-10 — 10 letters over 10 verses, so all 9 internal verse boundaries coincide with a letter start and 0 fall inside a letter; MT 112:9 and 112:10 carry 3 cola each, which is how 10 verses hold 22. This is the same defective warrant installed on the paired Ps 111 row; the campaign rule is that a shared cure is authored once and installed on both rows in the same pass, so the repair here and there is one edit.

reviews.reasoning: The seam at 113:4|113:5 is well chosen and I do not contest the span: MT 113:1 opens with the triple summons and MT 113:5 opens with the interrogative, a formally distinct unit-opener, and the row correctly discloses that the hallelu-Yah frame straddles its own seam (inventory: oshb:Ps.113.1 in the 11-member verse-initial list, oshb:Ps.113.9 in the 13-member verse-final list) rather than letting the cross-seam device argue silently against the cut. Confidence 'medium' is well calibrated. All 8 Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier (collate.py: 8 of 8 byte), check_marks.py is GREEN and pmarks_Ps.json shows no selah, K/Q or puncta in Ps 113; the 3 paseq segs in this psalm (MT 113:1, 113:4, 113:9) are seg-layer and correctly unclaimed. One evidence defect, repeated in two fields.

challenges.claim: In both the rationale and observed_substrate_signals the MT 113:4 quote stops one word short of its own gloss, which supplies a subject the quoted span does not contain.
challenges.evidence: The row quotes רָ֖ם עַל כָּל גּוֹיִ֥ם (oshb:Ps.113.4) and glosses it web:Ps.113.4 “Yahweh is high above all nations”, but the divine name is the next word: the span the gloss actually renders is רָ֖ם עַל כָּל גּוֹיִ֥ם יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.113.4). The cut point is defensible in itself — pmarks_Ps.json records 1 paseq in this verse and the row's cut falls at it — but then the gloss has to be re-cut to match, exactly as the row does correctly two clauses earlier, where its MT 113:2 quote and web:Ps.113.2 “Blessed be Yahweh’s name” cover the same span. Quote spans and their glosses cover the same span; expansion without a re-cut is the same regression as truncation.

reviews.reasoning: Re-derived independently and found sound. The opener is a genuine tier-1 register shift: MT 113:5 begins with the interrogative, which occurs in 0 of the 4 verses MT 113:1-113:4, and the row's own quote of it collates at BYTE tier. The close is inventory-exact: oshb:Ps.113.9 is a member of the 13-entry verse-final hallelu-Yah list in psalm_device_inventory.json and oshb:Ps.113.1 a member of the 11-entry verse-initial list, so both figures the row cites are the inventory's own and both memberships check out; the row also discloses that the frame brackets the psalm across its own seam rather than using the frame as silent evidence for the cut. All 6 Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier (collate.py), including the 2 participial forms, and the participial-chain reading cannot be machine-confirmed because the staged extract carries no morphology layer — but it is consistent with the pointed bytes and with both witnesses' renderings (web:Ps.113.6 “who stoops down to see”, web:Ps.113.7 “He raises up the poor out of the dust”), which is the standard the toolkit sets for form claims here. check_refs_mirror.py is GREEN: the out-of-span verse argued in prose (MT 113:1) is carried in boundary_evidence_refs as the web:Ps.113.1-Ps.113.4 range. pmarks_Ps.json shows no selah, K/Q, inverted nun, suspended letter or puncta anywhere in Ps 113, so no disclosure is owed; the paseq at MT 113:9 is seg-layer and is not claimed. rejected_alternative is one sentence and rules out the 113:5-6 / 113:7-9 rival on a textual ground (the continuous descriptive chain) rather than on taste. Confidence 'medium' is appropriate: the interrogative opener is a clean tier-1 signal but the psalm is short enough that a whole_psalm rival is not unreasonable, and the row does not overclaim. One observation, not a defect: the chain the row describes actually begins in MT 113:5 itself, one word after the interrogative, which strengthens rather than weakens the row's own boundary.

Re-derived and found sound, including the two claims most likely to be wrong. First, the untitled claim: verse_map_web.json has no Ps.114.0 pseudo-verse and Ps 114 is absent from the 116-entry superscription inventory, so 'no WEB title pseudo-verse' is exact, and the psalm is an identity psalm so web and MT verse numbers coincide 1:1 across the span. Second, the discourse-person claim, which the parallel Ps 110 rows get wrong: here it is correct — MT 114:1-114:4 carry 0 second-person forms, and the shift is abrupt at MT 114:5, where the same sea-and-Jordan pair returns as direct address (web:Ps.114.5 “What was it, you sea, that you fled?” against web:Ps.114.3 “The sea saw it, and fled”). Both Hebrew runs in the rationale and both in the signals collate at BYTE tier, and the quote/gloss spans match in each case. The row's cross-seam disclosure is right too: it names the vocabulary recurrence at MT 114:5 as its own seam's counter-pressure instead of leaving it unstated. pmarks_Ps.json records 0 entries of any mark class in Ps 114 — no selah, no paseq, no K/Q, no puncta — so there is no disclosure obligation and no mark-based rival seam to weigh. check_tiling.py confirms the 114:4|114:5 cut leaves the psalm exactly covered by the two rows. A rival 2+2+2+2 segmentation is arguable on parallelism but has no tier-1 warrant that competes with a clean report-to-apostrophe turn, and row policy does not favour it. Confidence 'high' is calibrated.

The span is right and I do not contest it: the apostrophe opened at MT 114:5 runs unbroken through MT 114:7, the vocabulary repetition against MT 114:3-114:4 is byte-visible, and the row correctly treats MT 114:8 as description rather than address without letting that force a further cut. All 7 Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier (collate.py: 7 of 7 byte), quote/gloss spans match, check_web_quotes.py is GREEN across the row's 3 curly-quoted WEB segments, and pmarks_Ps.json records no marks of any class in Ps 114, so nothing is owed by way of disclosure. Two smaller defects: a signal that locates a form where it is not, and a device_notes sentence that names a campaign authoring artifact in row prose. Confidence 'high' is defensible on the seam itself.

challenges.claim: The signal 'imperative form opening [the MT 114:7 quote] addresses the earth directly' places the imperative at the opening of a span that opens with a preposition two words earlier.
challenges.evidence: The quoted run begins מִלִּפְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן (oshb:Ps.114.7, web:Ps.114.7 “at the presence of the Lord”); the form that addresses the earth is the third word, in ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ (oshb:Ps.114.7, web:Ps.114.7 “Tremble, you earth”). The substance is right — MT 114:7 does turn the address from the waters and mountains to the earth — but the signal as written locates the form at the head of the verse, and the staged extract carries no morphology layer, so a form claim has to be argued from the pointed bytes and both renderings at the position it actually occupies. Note that the WEB word order inverts the Hebrew here, which is why the position needs stating rather than assuming.

challenges.claim: device_notes names a campaign authoring artifact in row prose ('the seam the part brief flags as this psalm's structural hinge'), which the register rule bans from row prose.
challenges.evidence: The register rule excludes decision-ids, strategy-section citations, erratum narration, positional row references, file-order talk and review-actor names from row prose EVER; naming 'the part brief' is the same class of pipeline reference and says nothing about the text. ngram7.py shows the construction is not a one-off: the 7-gram 'web ps is the seam the part' recurs across 2 rows in this cluster, so the cure is one edit installed on each affected row. The textual fact the sentence wants is already established in the row's own rationale by the byte-visible turn at MT 114:5, glossed web:Ps.114.5 “What was it, you sea, that you fled?”.
